Frederick Brown, presiding elder of the Methodist mission in Tien Tsin, who guided the allied forces into the Chinese capital. Mr. Brown who arrived here on the Coppt., was in Pekin at the time of the Boxer outbreak and was one of the last persons to leave that city before communication with the outside world had been cut off. But as he was refused passage by the military authorities, he succeeded in getting through on an American gunboat. As he was familiar with the city of Pekin, his advice was asked regarding the best means of entry, and it was on his suggestion that the sewer under the city's wall was chosen by the Americans and British. The result of this was their arrival several hours before the Russians and Japanese.

In relating his experiences, Dr. Brown said:

The capture of Tien Tsin on July 1st by the allied forces was so unexpected that the various yamens and ministries did not have time to hide their treasures or destroy their documents. Chicago, Dec. 3.—Four men and one boy were instantly killed, and twelve people injured by the explosion of a boiler in the power house at the Chicago and North-western Road this evening. Several of the injured are hurt so badly that they may die this date.

August Clammau, section foreman, crushed by falling walls; Anthony Krauz, fireman, internally injured, died on the way to the hospital; August Weiss, section hand, struck by boiler; Joseph Shechi, section hand, caught under boiler; Henry Schnur, 15 years old, dies in audit office, Northwestern road, neck broken by flying debris.

The injured are John Elttert, chief electrician of the power house, skull broken; August Heck, Milwaukee, injured by part of roof of parlor car; Mr. August Er, Milwaukee, thrown against seat, internally injured, may die; William Bicket, Chicago, Wis., severely bruised; Mrs. Ethel Becker, Chicago, Wis., slightly bruised; Michael McGregor, severely burned, may die; Joseph Koyrlski, severely burned; George Glie, severely burned; John Brown, severely burned; Carl Peters, arm broken; August Holtz, side and arm bruised; Eugene Gingellch, blown through door of power house, slightly bruised.

The power house was a two-story structure, which stood west of the passenger station and north of the tracks leading into it. On the first floor was the boiler room.

The cause of the explosion is a mystery, as everything in the boiler room seemed to be in excellent condition.

At 11:15 minutes past 8 o'clock one of the boilers in the center of the row burst with a detonation that was plainly heard 30 points aloft. One end of the boiler went toward the depot tracks and landed seventy feet away. The boiler itself, which weighed ten tons, lies tonight six feet from the boiler house. Just as the explosion occurred the Ashland limited train was pulling out of the station.

The last two cars were caught. The boiler struck the rear car, while the boiler-head ploughed through the one immediately in front. Fortunately both flew high, carrying away portions of the roof and vestibule. The injured passengers were struck by flying splinters, or thrown violently to the floor. Traffic was interrupted for several hours. The destruction of the electric lighting plant plunged the depot into darkness, and the piles of debris which were thrown across the tracks temporarily blocked the SUBURBAN traffic of the road.

The wounded were conveyed as quickly as possible to hospitals.

The property loss to the road will not be far from $4,000.
